papers.title: Alignment by Socialization: Learning Tradeoffs Under Selection
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) agents are expected to complete tasks while following rules of conduct, but these objectives can conflict. We study how evolutionary selection shapes an agent's choices between them, and whether experience can make those choices reflect human judgments and withstand subsequent pressures. In our model, copies of an agent face a common uncertain reward state, and only those taking the rewarded action reproduce. We show that long-run growth is maximized when each action is taken as often as the environment rewards it. We compare three policies. A task-only policy thrives in a sandbox rewarding completion alone but fails when conduct matters. A fixed linear policy increasingly favors task completion as its stakes rise, even where humans never reward it. A learned policy instead converges to the tradeoffs rewarded by its environment; when humans supply the rewards, we call this socialization. Accumulated experience makes socialization harder to reverse under subsequent task-only training, although violations can arise before the prevailing disposition changes, and finite memory weakens this protection. When a single violation can end a deployment, a hard prohibition can prevent it, but a mistaken prohibition can also be costly. Experiments with small neural networks illustrate how training targets and memory shape these outcomes. Our results suggest that alignment depends not only on the objectives assigned to agents, but also on the environments that shape and sustain their behavior.

papers.title: Who Pays for the Knowledge Models Copy? Model Collapse as Lossy Transmission and Rogers' Paradox
papers.abstract: Generative models trained on the output of earlier models lose knowledge across generations, rare knowledge first. The remedies that work all bring in information from outside the loop, such as fresh human data, verifiers, or curators, and the theory of model collapse treats that supply as given. We argue that cultural evolution has a theory of the supply, and that it distinguishes two ways copying loses knowledge. In a fixed world, copies are lossy, as in Henrich's account of skill loss in small populations. In a changing world, even perfect copies go stale, which is Rogers' paradox. We write both as one chain with separately measurable parameters and test it on lineages of language models (word trigrams and a character transformer on two books, and OPT-125m on wikitext-2, on arXiv abstracts written after its pretraining, and on a world of 2,000 fictional facts that change at a set rate). In a fixed world, neutral drift on word frequencies predicts, with no free parameter, the rare-word coverage of every trigram lineage to within 0.03. In the fact world, the model's accuracy falls and its outdated answers rise with the rate of change; the chain calibrated on the static world predicts both for mid- and low-frequency facts to within 0.03 on average, with the rate of change set, not fitted. Models that inherit their weights keep more in a static world and carry more outdated facts in a changing one, as Rogers' theory says of individual memory. Finally we close the loop with the people who write the data. When they can ask the model instead of finding out, the model ends up exactly as reliable as finding out is costly, and in both regimes someone must keep paying to learn; we give the share in closed form, extend it to lossy copying, heterogeneous costs, aggregating models, and users who check, and show when checking is a stable way out.

papers.title: Extending indoor airborne infection risk modelling to 3D, with local surface deposition
papers.abstract: Mathematical models of indoor airborne disease transmission often rely on simplifying assumptions to reduce computational cost. In particular, aerosol concentrations may be assumed uniform across room height, allowing a two-dimensional (2D) formulation, while particle deposition on surfaces is represented by a first-order removal term acting throughout the computational domain. Here, we investigate how these assumptions affect predictions of airborne infection risk. We extend the Viral Infection Risk Indoor Simulator (VIRIS) [Xue et al. 2024] by developing a three-dimensional (3D) reaction-diffusion formulation in which aerosol deposition is represented by local removal at surfaces through a Robin boundary condition. We compare the original VIRIS framework with the extended model (VIRIS-3D-L) across three indoor spaces of increasing architectural and people-movement complexity: a courtroom, a care home and a supermarket. Across all three settings, the original 2D formulation with global removal predicts lower infection risks than the 3D formulation with local deposition, with differences of up to 50%. The predictions of VIRIS-3D-L also show encouraging agreement with observations from a documented courtroom outbreak previously used to validate VIRIS. Although computation time increases by approximately a factor of four on average, simulations remain feasible on a standard laptop, taking between 7 minutes and just over two hours. These findings suggest that VIRIS-3D-L offers a more physically realistic framework for assessing indoor airborne infection risk without prohibitive computational costs, while the original VIRIS remains useful when rapid simulations are required.

papers.title: Bayesian Comparison of Covid Origins Hypotheses
papers.abstract: Applying standard Bayesian methods to the most reliably known unclassified facts about the Covid epidemic allows crude estimation of the odds for research-related vs. purely zoonotic origins. Here a broadly inclusive zoonotic hypothesis is compared with a rather specific subset of the research-related hypothesis defined by known prior work and grant proposals. The important observations are the type of virus, the city of the first outbreak, the lack of known prior hosts, the anomalous early pattern of evolution, and two specific features of the viral sequence. The resulting odds strongly favor research. The odds remain fairly strong under inclusion of uncertainties in prior odds.

papers.title: From life-history model to theories of ecological diversity: the impact of Madhav Gadgil's work
papers.abstract: In this article, we review and provide perspectives on the foundational contributions of the renowned ecologist Madhav Gadgil, including the Gadgil-Bossert life-history model, ecological diversity, population biology, harvesting theory, human-ecological systems, co-evolution, adaptive management, and environmental democracy. We take the Gadgil-Bossert model of reproductive allocation as a starting point for reviewing Gadgil's broader contributions to evolutionary and population theory. Then we examine how density regulation shapes selection on reproductive allocation in his work on $r$- and $K$-selection. We then consider how interactions among genotypes determine whether a mixture can remain stable and resist invasion. We outline the key theoretical developments arising from these works and discuss their continued influence on contemporary ecological thought and present-day ecological systems.
